title: Weekly links October 15: what does a coach do, beyond services vs manufacturing, what DiD to use, migration and jobs, and more…
gist: A weekly links roundup from the World Bank's Development Impact blog covering the roles of coaching in graduation programs, an argument that factories no longer anchor development, migration as a jobs solution, a DiD estimator tool, Egypt's educated-youth mismatch and AI use in lab experiments.

insights.claim: Francisco Amodio argues that countries attracting modern factories and exporting no longer see the broad-based employment growth of earlier industrialization, so factories should perhaps no longer sit at the center of development strategies.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Export-led manufacturing may deliver fewer jobs, weakening a classic EM growth template.

insights.claim: Amodio argues non-tradable services cannot generate virtuous cycles large, broad and predictable enough to anchor a national development strategy, because manufacturing historically raised ordinary workers' productivity at scale.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Services-led growth is not a ready substitute for manufacturing in this view.
insights.quote: Manufacturing’s historical contribution was that, in raising the productivity of firms, it raised the productivity of ordinary workers, at scale.

insights.claim: Industrial policy should ask which sectors create opportunities for everyone else, since the sectors that matter most may not create jobs themselves but trigger chains of investment, production and consumption beyond their boundaries.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Sector selection should be judged on multiplier effects, not direct employment.

insights.claim: Dany Bahar argues that without migration rich democracies would lose 121 million working-age people between 2020 and 2050 while Africa and South Asia together gain over a billion, so many jobs development institutions want to create already exist in other countries.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Demographic mismatch supports labor-mobility policies; connecting them requires visas, language preparation and qualification recognition.

insights.claim: Patricia Andrews Fearon and Mahreen Khan identify four roles of coaching in graduation programs (aspirational, behavioral and skill building, relational, administrative), some more easily scaled or replaced by technology than others.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Technology substitution is more feasible for some coaching roles, shaping cost-effective scaling.
insights.locator: What is the magic sauce in coaching?

insights.claim: Clement de Chaisemartin shared a dashboard and a Stata command, whichDIDshouldIuse, that characterize a researcher's difference-in-differences design and suggest estimators.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Helps researchers choose valid DiD estimators.
insights.locator: What DiD estimator should you use?

insights.claim: On the ETRM blog Francisco Flores shares experiences using Claude Code to assist data collection for a lab experiment.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Development economists are adopting AI coding agents in field and lab research workflows.
insights.locator: Using AI to enhance your survey instrument

insights.claim: A J-PAL piece on Egypt's labor market mismatch concludes training should change, but the post's author argues it also needs focus on entrepreneurship, competition policy and raising demand for educated labor.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Supply-side training fixes alone leave demand-side constraints on educated-youth jobs unaddressed.
